headline: A space telescope finds a new comet by accident

sources.title: New comet accidentally discovered by space telescope (Popular Science)
We've got a new comet in our skies. And it's the first ever discovered by a brand new space telescope (BBC Sky at Night Magazine)

chunks.text: On October 19, 2026, the European Space Agency shared some surprising news. Its Euclid space telescope had found a [[brand new]] comet [[by accident]]. Euclid was built to take deep, [[steady]] pictures of [[distant]] galaxies, not to follow [[fast-moving]] comets. It usually {{stays away from}} the part of the sky where most comets and asteroids are. Even so, a comet {{showed up}} in pictures taken between September 16 and 24.

verbs.correct: To avoid an area by choice
verbs.wrong: To take blurry pictures of an area
verbs.why: Many people stay away from the beach in winter. Our dog stays away from the busy road. Euclid usually stays away from the part of the sky where most comets and asteroids are.

verbs.correct: To become visible in a picture
verbs.wrong: To shine brighter than the stars
verbs.why: Dust often shows up in old photos. A small bird shows up in the corner of the picture. A comet showed up in Euclid's pictures taken between September 16 and 24.

chunks.text: A researcher at the University of Helsinki in Finland [[made the discovery]]. He wrote software that searches Euclid's pictures for moving objects. The software {{picked out}} a [[streak]] across several images. He guessed where the object would be next and {{tracked it down}} in other pictures. [[A closer look]] revealed a [[fuzzy]] cloud around it. That cloud is a sign of a comet {{giving off}} dust and gas.

verbs.correct: To find one thing among many
verbs.why: She picks out her best friend in a big crowd. Good readers pick out the main idea quickly. The researcher's software picked out a streak across several images.
The police track down stolen cars with cameras. He tracks down old school friends online. The researcher guessed where the object would be next and tracked it down in other pictures.

verbs.wrong: To be made of gas or dust
verbs.why: Burning wood gives off smoke and ash. Old trucks give off a lot of dirty gas. The fuzzy cloud is a sign of a comet giving off dust and gas.

chunks.text: The researcher then checked lists of known comets and asteroids. There was [[no match]], so he could {{rule out}} a known object. He reported it to an international center that [[keeps track of]] comets and asteroids. The center {{passed the news along}} to astronomers around the world. Astronomers on the ground {{followed up}} with their own [[observations]]. On October 8, the center [[confirmed]] that the object is a new comet.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To add a new name to a list
verbs.why: Doctors rule out a broken bone with an X-ray. The police rule out the neighbor because he was at work. There was no match in the lists, so the researcher could rule out a known object.

verbs.wrong: To check that a report is true
verbs.why: Teachers pass the news along to parents by email. My mom passes along tips from her doctor. The international center passed the news along to astronomers around the world.

verbs.correct: To do more to check something
verbs.why: Doctors follow up with more tests after a strange result. Reporters follow up with more questions after a speech. Astronomers on the ground followed up with their own observations.

chunks.text: The comet is about 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth. The planets all [[circle]] the Sun at about the same level, but this comet does not. Instead, it [[arches]] high over the solar system. One trip around the Sun takes thousands of years. Astronomers need more [[data]] to {{find out}} exactly how long. Tracking comets also helps the team {{clean up}} its pictures of galaxies. A scientist on the team {{pointed out}} that Euclid is expected to find very few comets. He called this one a [[happy coincidence]].

verbs.correct: To learn a fact you did not know
verbs.why: Students find out their grades online. I call the store to find out when it opens. Astronomers need more data to find out exactly how long one trip around the Sun takes.

verbs.correct: To remove unwanted spots from images
verbs.wrong: To make copies of image files
verbs.why: Photo apps clean up old pictures with dust spots. My brother cleans up his photos before he prints them. Tracking comets also helps the Euclid team clean up its pictures of galaxies.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.wrong: To write a long science report
verbs.why: My teacher points out my spelling mistakes. Doctors often point out that sleep is important. A scientist on the team pointed out that Euclid is expected to find very few comets.

mainIdea.s: A European telescope built to photograph faraway galaxies spotted an unknown comet by chance. A Finnish researcher's software noticed it, and experts later confirmed the find.
mainIdea.why: Euclid was built to take pictures of distant galaxies, yet a comet showed up in them. A researcher's software picked it out, and a center confirmed it on October 8.

mainIdea.s: A space telescope caught a new comet in its images without even trying. Astronomers using ground telescopes saw it first, then asked the space team to search its pictures for it.
mainIdea.why: Close, but a researcher's software found the comet in Euclid's pictures first. Astronomers on the ground followed up later with their own observations.

mainIdea.s: Scientists in Europe say a large comet will pass close to Earth next spring. They expect people in many countries to see its bright tail with their own eyes for several weeks.
mainIdea.why: Euclid found a new, faraway comet by accident. A researcher's software picked out a streak in its pictures, and the find was confirmed on October 8.

tf.s: A comet showed up in pictures from a telescope built to study galaxies.
tf.why: Euclid was built to take steady pictures of distant galaxies, but a new comet showed up in its images.

tf.s: Euclid was designed to search the sky for new comets.
tf.why: It was built to photograph distant galaxies, and it usually stays away from the part of the sky with most comets.

tf.s: A researcher's software picked out a streak across several images.
tf.why: His software searches Euclid's pictures for moving objects, and it picked out the streak.

tf.s: The fuzzy cloud around the object showed it was an asteroid.
tf.why: The fuzzy cloud is a sign of a comet giving off dust and gas.

tf.s: Astronomers on the ground followed up with their own observations.
tf.why: The center passed the news along to astronomers around the world, and they checked the object too.

tf.s: The new comet matched one that scientists already had on their lists.
tf.why: There was no match in the lists, so the researcher could rule out a known object.

lines.text: Did you hear that a space telescope found a new comet by accident?
By accident? How does a telescope find a comet by accident?
It's a European telescope called Euclid. It takes pictures of faraway galaxies, and it usually {{stays away from}} the part of the sky with lots of comets.
So how did a comet {{show up}} in its pictures?
It was a [[lucky break]]. A researcher in Finland wrote software that searches the pictures for anything moving.
Yes. It {{picked out}} a thin streak across several images. Then he {{tracked it down}} in other pictures.
Wow, that's [[no small feat]]. He must be really good at his job.
Then he saw a fuzzy cloud around it. That means it's a comet {{giving off}} dust and gas.
Couldn't it be a comet that people already knew about?
He checked the lists and {{ruled that out}}.
So who decides that it's real?
An international center. It {{passed the news along}}, and astronomers on the ground {{followed up}}. They confirmed it on October 8.
That was fast. They're really [[on the ball]].
They are. And remember, the telescope wasn't even trying to find comets.
[[How cool is that]]? So what do they still want to {{find out}}?
How long one trip around the Sun takes. It's thousands of years, but they need more data to say exactly.
Wow. I guess the lesson is to [[keep your eyes open]].

expressions.def: Used to show that you think something is exciting or great
